lesson.title: Reading One Number Off a Curve
lesson.summary: Treats f prime of a as a single real number carrying local steepness information, and works a square-root example using conjugate multiplication when simple expansion is not enough.
lesson.body:
The derivative at a point, f prime of a, is a single real number attached to a single input value a. It is easy to lose sight of this simplicity once formulas get complicated, so it is worth stating plainly: f prime of a answers the question "how fast is f changing exactly at x = a," and the answer is one number, no more mysterious than knowing that f(a) itself is one number. Different points on the same curve generally give different values of f prime of a, because a curve can be steep in one place and flatter in another; that variation is exactly what makes it interesting.

Computing f prime of a always starts from the same limit definition covered previously, but the algebra needed to evaluate the limit depends heavily on what kind of function you have. Polynomials usually just need expansion and cancellation of an h. Functions involving square roots often need a different trick: multiplying by a conjugate expression to clear the root before the limit can be evaluated directly.

Here is that technique in action. Let f(x) equal the square root of x, and find f prime of 4. By definition, f prime of 4 equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [square root of (4 + h) minus square root of 4] divided by h, and the square root of 4 is 2, so the numerator is square root of (4 + h) minus 2. Plugging h = 0 directly gives 0 divided by 0, so more work is needed. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate, square root of (4 + h) plus 2: the numerator becomes [square root of (4 + h) minus 2] times [square root of (4 + h) plus 2], which is a difference of squares equal to (4 + h) minus 4, or just h. The full expression is now h divided by [h times (square root of (4 + h) plus 2)]. The h in the numerator cancels the h in the denominator, valid since h is not 0 in the limit, leaving 1 divided by [square root of (4 + h) plus 2]. Now substitution is safe: as h approaches 0, this becomes 1 divided by (square root of 4 plus 2), which is 1 divided by (2 plus 2), or 1 fourth. So f prime of 4 equals one fourth.

That result says the graph of the square root function is rising, but gently, at x = 4: for every 4 units you move right near that point, the curve rises roughly 1 unit. Compare this to the steep polynomial examples from earlier sections, where derivatives at a point came out as whole numbers like 6 or 12; here the derivative at a point is a fraction, and that is perfectly normal.

The same conjugate technique applies at any positive input for the square root function, not just at 4. Repeating the steps with a general point a in place of 4 gives f prime of a equals 1 divided by (2 times the square root of a), a formula that reduces to one fourth exactly when a = 4, since 2 times the square root of 4 is 2 times 2, which is 4, and 1 divided by 4 is one fourth. This is a preview of the derivative function idea from the next section: the same limit machinery, run once with a variable in place of a fixed number, produces a formula valid at every point instead of just one.

The value of f prime of a carries real information about the local steepness of the graph, and the technique used to extract it, expand and cancel for polynomials, conjugate multiplication for roots, is chosen to defeat whatever is causing the 0 over 0 problem in that specific case. Recognizing which trick a given function needs is itself a skill worth practicing.
